Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses and can present atypically, closely mimicking acute pancreatitis (AP).
analysis.methods: A single 33‑year‑old man was evaluated; clinical data, laboratory tests (including platelet count and renal function), contrast‑enhanced CT imaging, and whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) were performed.
analysis.results: The patient had fever, vomiting, diarrhea, profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, mild pancreatic changes with progressive retroperitoneal exudation and pleural effusion on CT, and mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (plus hepatitis B virus); he recovered with supportive care and IVIG, and follow‑up ultrasound showed a normal pancreas.
analysis.contribution: The report demonstrates that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely resemble severe AP, identifies key diagnostic clues (disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal signs, preserved pancreatic parenchyma), and shows that mNGS enables rapid pathogen confirmation to guide appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: The evidence is limited to an abstract of a single case; no broader epidemiologic data, detailed location, or long‑term outcomes are provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by orthohantaviruses can mimic acute pancreatitis. Methods: A 33‑year‑old patient underwent clinical assessment, labs, contrast CT, and whole‑blood mNGS. Results: He presented with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, severe thrombocytopenia (29 × 10⁹/L), renal impairment, mild pancreatic changes, progressive retroperitoneal exudation, pleural effusion, and mNGS detected high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered with supportive care and IVIG, and follow‑up ultrasound was normal. Contribution: Highlights diagnostic clues differentiating Seoul orthohantavirus infection from severe pancreatitis and demonstrates mNGS utility for early pathogen confirmation. papers.title: Hantavirus on a Cruise Ship: What COVID-19 Taught Us.
papers.abstract: Delayed recognition of the mechanics of aerosol transmission-the primary mode of spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-at the beginning of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic led to inadequate early recommendations regarding nonpharmaceutical interventions and poor initial messaging about how to reduce infection risk. We highlight key epidemiological details of Andes virus (ANDV) transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and during prior reported outbreaks with confirmed person-to-person spread in Argentina, which, together, suggest aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of transmission of ANDV between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissible environmental settings.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

papers.title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. METHODS: Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. FINDINGS: Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. INTERPRETATION: Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. FUNDING: Defense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. Methods Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). papers.title: Dual-Target Inhibition of Puumala Virus Entry Glycoproteins Gn and Gc by Moringa oleifera -Derived Phytochemicals: An Integrated Computational Study
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), a member of the Orthohantavirus genus, causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate type of hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, yet no approved antiviral therapy is currently available. Viral entry is initiated by the coordinated actions of the attachment glycoprotein Gn and fusion glycoprotein Gc, making simultaneous inhibition of these proteins an attractive antiviral strategy. Here, we employed a combined computational workflow to identify dual-target inhibitors of PUUV entry glycoproteins from Moringa oleifera phytochemicals. 72 phytochemicals were retrieved and docked by molecular docking to identify high-affinity binders, while he top-ranked compounds were subsequently evaluated for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behavior, toxicity, and predicted biological activities to assess their therapeutic suitability. Complex stability and binding mechanisms were further investigated through 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations (MDS) and MM-GBSA binding free-energy calculations. Quercetin and kaempferol showed the lowest binding energies toward Gn (−9.8 and −9.7 kcal/mol) and Gc (−10.4 and −10.0 kcal/mol), respectively. Both phytochemicals demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, high gastrointestinal absorption, no predicted toxicity, and positive bioactivity scores. MDS confirmed stable protein–ligand complexes with minimal structural fluctuations, and MM-GBSA analysis further validated strong binding, with quercetin exhibiting the most favorable binding free energies against Gn (−84.24 kcal/mol) and Gc (−98.45 kcal/mol). These findings identify quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual-target inhibitors that may simultaneously disrupt PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, warranting further experimental validation.

analysis_zh.methods: 作者采用集成计算工作流程:将72种辣木(Moringa oleifera)植物化学物质对PUUV Gn和Gc蛋白进行对接,筛选出最优结合物进行药物相似性和ADMET评估,随后对最佳候选物进行100 ns分子动力学模拟和MM-GBSA自由能计算(A3、A4、A5)。

analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究确定槲皮素和槲皮素酮为普马拉病毒入侵的潜在双靶点抑制剂,为后续实验验证提供候选分子(A9)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究仅基于计算分析;未提供实验或临床数据,证据仅限于摘要(abstract_only)。

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

papers.full_text: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome Xiaojiao Li 1,2,3, Lin Su 2,3, Yinli He 2,3, Linpei Zhang 2,3, Tianyan Chen 1*, Minhong Fei 4* and Yawen Wang 2,3,5* 1Infectious Diseases Department, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 2BioBank, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 3Shaanxi Engineering Research Center for Biobank and Advanced Medical Research, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 4Jiangyan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Taizhou, Jiangsu, China, 5Department of Laboratory Medicine, First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving out- comes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratifi- cation. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine labo- ratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS. KEYWORDS biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS 1 Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute infectious disease caused by several Orthohantavirus species in the family Hantaviridae. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corre- sponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5). Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to b3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation dis- turbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9). Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechan- ical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes. In recent years, research on early warning of severe HFRS has advanced considerably across multiple levels, encompassing bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging novel biomarkers. In this review, we comprehensively synthesize progress in the aforementioned areas and evaluate the predictive performance and translational potential of various bio- markers. We also discuss current challenges and future perspec- tives, with the aim of establishing an evidence base for early identification and precise management of severe HFRS. 2 Clinically accessible warning systems for early risk stratification Clinically accessible warning systems including bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters are the most important indicators for predicting severe HFRS. This section reviews the available evidence on bedside signs and standard laboratory tests for predicting severe HFRS. The goal is to provide a practical frame- work for early risk assessment. 2.1 Bedside signs of severe HFRS prediction Bedside signs offer unique discriminative value for early risk stratification in HFRS, particularly in the absence of laboratory data. The 2021 Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Treatment of HFRS identifies several key warning indicators for severe cases. These include a history of travel to endemic areas or contact with rodents and their excreta within two months prior to onset, high fever (temperature >40 °C or febrile duration exceeding one week), severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as intense nausea and vomiting, psychiatric disturbances including agitation or delirium, marked conjunctival edema, and obvious bleeding tendency (10). Regarding imaging findings, a retrospective analysis by Huang et al. of 191 patients with HFRS in southwestern China demonstrated that pleural effusion was an independent risk factor for progression to severe HFRS. Patients with pleural effusion had a 4.49-fold higher risk of severe progression compared to those without it, suggesting that this sign may reflect more extensive capillary leakage and systemic inflammation (14). The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score also has shown significant value in predicting severe HFRS. Ma and colleagues conducted a multicenter study of 551 HFRS patients in Hubei Province. They demonstrated that an admission qSOFA score of 2 or higher was an independent risk factor for 30-day mortality. The qSOFA score is defined as meeting any two of the following criteria: respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, or altered mental status. This finding suggests that the qSOFA score, without reliance on any laboratory tests, can serve as a rapid triage tool for early identification of high- risk HFRS patients and for determining the need for intensive care unit admission (19). Notably, the early warning indicators for severe HFRS vary across different age groups. Researchers at Tangdu Hospital have conducted stratified warning analyses for both older adults and children (20, 21). In the older-adult cohort (≥60 years), Li et al. reviewed 146 cases and identified several early warning signs using multivariate logistic regression. These included chest tightness or dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, decreased urine output (UO), skin and mucosal hemorrhage, and phase overlap (disease course span- ning two or more typical phases). These findings suggest that assessment of older adults with HFRS should focus more on cardiopulmonary function, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal perfu- sion, coagulation status, and disease progression patterns (20). In the pediatric cohort (<16 years), the same group analyzed 103 cases. They found that conjunctival edema, hypotensive shock, and elevated serum creatinine (Cr) were key early warning indicators. This suggests that assessment in children should focus more on fluid extravasation, circulatory status, and early renal changes. Taken together, risk assessment should combine exposure history, consensus-based warning signs, bedside scores, and age-specific findings (21). Li et al. 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1986264 Frontiers in Immunology frontiersin.org 02 2.2 Routine laboratory parameters for early warning of severe HFRS 2.2.1 Blood cell indices and inflammatory markers Blood count and routine inflammatory markers are the most accessible laboratory indicators for evaluating the systemic host response in HFRS. Markedly elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and severely reduced platelet count (PLT) have long been recog- nized as warning signs for HFRS severity (11, 22). The 2021 Expert Consensus has established WBC >30 × 109/L and PLT <20 × 109/L as definitive severity warning thresholds (10). This pattern has been consistently confirmed by multiple retrospective cohort studies from various regions. Yang et al. analyzed 109 HFRS cases in central China and found that the median WBC in the severe group (25.2 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the mild group (12.6 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the mild group (54 × 109/L) (12). Chen et al. further examined the association between these two indicators and adverse outcomes in a cohort of 395 HFRS patients in northwestern China. The results showed that the median WBC in the non-survivor group (23.19 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the survivor group (13.29 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the survivor group (41 × 109/L) (23). Platelet distribution width (PDW) may provide infor- mation on platelet activation and function beyond that conveyed by PLT alone. Fan et al. studied 260 HFRS patients and found that PDW on the first day of admission increased significantly with disease severity. Of note, in critically ill patients, the association between PDW and prognosis was reversed, with non-survivors exhibiting lower PDW than survivors. This reversal may reflect exhausted marrow hematopoietic compensation, where declining PDW portends worse outcomes (24). The neutrophil-to-red blood cell ratio (NRR) and neutrophil- to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), as simple readouts of systemic inflam- mation, have demonstrated predictive value across multiple viral species. Xiao et al. analyzed 342 HTNV-HFRS cases in Xi’an and found that NRR was significantly elevated in the severe/critical group, with optimal discriminative performance for severity grad- ing, whereas NLR was significantly elevated in the non-survivor group, with optimal performance for 28-day all-cause mortality prediction. Both markers are accessible at the bedside, with NRR more suitable for early severity stratification and NLR better aligned with mortality risk assessment (25). In PUUV infection, Nusshag et al. analyzed 32 PUUV-infected patients in Germany and showed that peak NLR was significantly elevated in severe patients with hospitalization exceeding five days, suggesting that systemic neu- trophil-lymphocyte imbalance is an important accompanying fea- ture of PUUV severity (26). Procalcitonin (PCT), as an indicator reflecting the severity of infection and inflammation, has shown predictive value across multiple independent studies. Duan et al. found that serum PCT level at emergency department admission was an independent risk factor for severe progression in HFRS patients, with the median PCT in the severe group significantly higher than in the mild group (8.12 vs. 1.39 ng/mL); an admission PCT exceeding 2.97 ng/mL demonstrated good predictive value for severity, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.862, and a sensitivity of 88.0% (27). Chen et al. found in 272 HFRS patients that admission PCT levels increased significantly with disease severity, with an AUC of 0.792 for predicting 28-day survival/ death at an optimal cutoff of 2.28 ng/mL, outperforming WBC (AUC 0.769) (28). Che et al. further confirmed in a retrospective study of 373 HFRS patients that the median admission PCT in the severe group was significantly higher than in the mild group (3.8 vs. 1.3 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.824 for predicting severity; PCT was also significantly higher in non-survivors than in survivors (3.6 vs. 1.7 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.737 for predicting hospital mortality (7). Huang et al. confirmed in a retrospective cohort of 191 HFRS patients in southwestern China that PCT was an independent risk factor for severe progression, with each 1 ng/mL increase in PCT associated with approximately 33% higher odds of developing severe disease (14). Yu et al. also confirmed in a cohort of 384 HFRS patients that PCT was significantly higher in the severe/ critical group than in the mild/moderate group, with multivariate logistic regression confirming elevated PCT as an independent predictor of severe progression (29). These results indicate that PCT is a useful marker for assessing both disease severity and short- term mortality in HFRS, and may help identify high-risk pa- tients early. Unlike PCT, C-reactive protein (CRP) showed limited inde- pendent value for HFRS severity prediction. Che et al. studied 373 HFRS patients and found that admission CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (median 42.1 vs. 29.5 mg/L). However, its AUC for severity prediction was only 0.614, far below that of PCT (0.824) (7). Yang et al. also found that although the median CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (51.0 vs. 30.9 mg/L), CRP was deemed to lack independent incremental value during least absolute shrink- age and selection operator (LASSO) regression variable selection and was therefore not included in the final prediction model (12). Chen et al. further confirmed in 272 HFRS patients that admission CRP was elevated across all severity grades (mean approximately 30.1 to 33.96 mg/L for each group), with no statistically significant difference among the four groups, indicating that CRP does not exhibit a gradient change with disease severity. However, CRP retains potential utility in assessing secondary bacterial infection: the median CRP in the infected group was significantly higher than in the non-infected group (43.2 vs. 26.4 mg/L, p < 0.001), with an AUC of 0.588 for predicting secondary bacterial infection (p = 0.005). Although this represents moderate-to-weak performance, it is statistically significant, whereas PCT showed no discriminative capacity in this setting (28). Therefore, CRP is more suitable as an auxiliary marker for bacterial infection rather than an independent predictor of HFRS severity. The predictive role of serum albumin (ALB) and hemoglobin (Hb) remains controversial. The 2021 Expert Consensus lists serum ALB below 15 g/L as a severity warning indicator (10). Huang et al. reported that the median admission ALB was significantly lower in the severe group than in the mild group (25.45 vs. 29.80 g/L) on univariate analysis. full_text_sections.full_text: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome Xiaojiao Li 1,2,3, Lin Su 2,3, Yinli He 2,3, Linpei Zhang 2,3, Tianyan Chen 1*, Minhong Fei 4* and Yawen Wang 2,3,5* 1Infectious Diseases Department, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 2BioBank, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 3Shaanxi Engineering Research Center for Biobank and Advanced Medical Research, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 4Jiangyan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Taizhou, Jiangsu, China, 5Department of Laboratory Medicine, First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving out- comes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratifi- cation. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine labo- ratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS. KEYWORDS biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS 1 Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute infectious disease caused by several Orthohantavirus species in the family Hantaviridae. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corre- sponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5). Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to b3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation dis- turbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9). Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechan- ical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes. papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen mainly distributed in East Asia that causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans (A1, A2).
analysis.methods: The study employed an integrated bioinformatics pipeline to identify early‑stage HTNV‑related host interaction genes, screen natural compounds from the HERB database, and predict therapeutic mechanisms (A3).
analysis.results: Core up‑regulated genes CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were identified; six candidate natural compounds were retrieved, with quercetin emerging as the most promising due to high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and acceptable toxicity (A4, A6); molecular docking predicted favorable binding of quercetin to HTNV RdRp (Lys884, Arg892) (A11); baseline assays in uninfected HEK293T cells showed low cytotoxicity at 3.9‑7.8 µM and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3 and TNF (A10).
analysis.contribution: The work proposes quercetin as a hypothesis‑generating computational candidate to modulate HTNV‑related host responses and provides a framework for generating mechanistic hypotheses to support One Health surveillance and control (A12, A13).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on abstract‑level computational predictions and limited in‑vitro data, with no experimental validation of antiviral efficacy; the abstract‑only scope restricts detail on methods and results (A12).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV is a rodent‑borne zoonotic virus in East Asia causing severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. Methods: An integrated bioinformatics pipeline identified early‑stage host interaction genes, screened natural compounds, and predicted mechanisms. Results: CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were up‑regulated; quercetin was highlighted for favorable ADMET, docked to HTNV RdRp, and showed low cytotoxicity (3.9‑7.8 µM) with reduced BCL2, MAPK3, TNF expression in HEK293T cells. Limitations: Conclusions are based on abstract‑only computational and limited in‑vitro data without experimental validation.

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒 (HTNV) 是一种主要分布于东亚的啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,可导致人类严重的 肾综合征出血热(A1, A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用一体化生物信息学流程,识别早期 HTNV 相关的宿主相互作用基因,筛选 HERB 数据库中的天然化合物,并预测治疗机制(A3)。
analysis_zh.results: 鉴定出核心上调基因 CXCL10、STAT1 和 IL10;检索到六种候选天然化合物,槲皮素因预测的高胃肠道吸收率和可接受的毒性而被视为最有前景的(A4, A6);分子对接预测槲皮素与 HTNV RdRp(Lys884、Arg892)具有有利的结合(A11);在未感染的 HEK293T 细胞中的基线实验显示 3.9‐7.8 μM 槲皮素的细胞毒性低,并降低 BCL2、MAPK3 和 TNF 的转录(A10)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作提出将槲皮素作为生成假设的计算候选物,以调节 HTNV 相关的宿主反应,并提供了一个用于生成机制性假设以支持 One Health 监测与控制的框架(A12, A13)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果仅基于摘要层面的计算预测和有限的体外数据,缺乏抗病毒效力的实验验证;仅有摘要的范围限制了对方法和结果的细节描述(A12)。

papers.title: Integrated immunoinformatics and molecular dynamics approaches reveal a promising multi-epitope vaccine against hantavirus.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), with substantial global morbidity and mortality. No universally approved human vaccine exists, making a safe, effective vaccine a public health priority. An immunoinformatics strategy was used to design a multi-epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor (GP_HANTL) of Hantaan orthohantavirus. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and B-cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC-binding affinity, and population coverage. Selected epitopes were joined with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and fused to a β-defensin adjuvant. The construct was evaluated by physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization, and in silico cloning. The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, with 99.24% global population coverage. Structural validation showed 95% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82. Molecular docking produced a favorable ClusPro score (- 1273.6) for the selected MEVC-TLR4 complex. Immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses, including elevated antibodies, memory B cells, and CTL/HTL activation. Codon optimization yielded a CAI of 0.94, supporting efficient Escherichia coli expression. A 100-ns MD simulation showed substantial conformational adaptation of the MEVC while TLR4 remained comparatively stable; accompanying Rg and SASA trends indicated that the MEVC adopted a more compact state during the trajectory. The proposed MEVC demonstrated favorable predicted immunogenicity, favorable structural characteristics, broad population coverage, and favorable expression characteristics. These findings support experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against Hantavirus infection. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00782-6.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome, with substantial global morbidity and mortality (A1). No universally approved human vaccine exists, making vaccine development a public‑health priority (A2).
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics pipeline was applied to design a multi‑epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor of Hantaan orthohantavirus (A3); CTL, HTL and B‑cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC binding affinity and population coverage (A4); selected epitopes were linked with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG and KK linkers and fused to a β‑defensin adjuvant (A5); the construct was evaluated by physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization and in silico cloning (A6).
analysis.results: The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL and 5 B‑cell epitopes with 99.24 % global population coverage (A7); structural validation showed 95 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82 (A8); docking to TLR4 gave a favorable ClusPro score of –1273.6 (A9); immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses (A10); codon optimization yielded a CAI of 0.94 for E. coli expression (A11); a 100‑ns MD simulation showed the MEVC adopting a more compact state (decreasing Rg and SASA) while TLR4 remained stable (A12, A13).
analysis.contribution: The in silico findings indicate the MEVC has favorable predicted immunogenicity, structural stability, broad population coverage and expression potential, supporting experimental validation as a preventive strategy against hantavirus infection (A14, A15).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract and supplementary information are available; experimental validation, in vivo immunogenicity, and safety data are not reported (A16).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes severe disease worldwide and lacks an approved human vaccine, creating a public‑health need (A1, A2). Methods: Researchers used immunoinformatics to design a multi‑epitope vaccine targeting the Hantaan virus glycoprotein, predicting CTL, HTL and B‑cell epitopes, linking them with specific linkers and a β‑defensin adjuvant, and evaluating the construct via physicochemical, structural, docking, MD, immune simulation, codon optimization and in silico cloning (A3‑A6). Results: The final construct includes 10 CTL, 10 HTL and 5 B‑cell epitopes covering 99.24 % of the global population; 95 % of residues are in favored Ramachandran regions (ERRAT 82); docking to TLR4 gave a ClusPro score of –1273.6; immune simulation predicts strong humoral and cellular responses; codon optimization CAI is 0.94; MD shows the vaccine becomes more compact while TLR4 stays stable (A7‑A13). Contribution: The data suggest the vaccine is immunogenic, structurally stable, broadly applicable and expressible, warranting experimental testing (A14, A15). Limitations: Only abstract and supplementary material are provided; no experimental or in vivo validation is reported (A16).

papers.title_zh: 综合免疫信息学与分子动力学方法揭示针对 汉坦病毒 的有前景的多表位疫苗。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是一种啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热 和 汉坦病毒肺综合征,在全球范围内造成显著的发病率和死亡率 (A1)。目前尚无普遍获批的人用疫苗,使疫苗研发成为公共卫生的重点任务 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用免疫信息学流程设计针对汉滩病毒 正汉坦病毒 (A3) 糖蛋白前体的多表位疫苗构建体(MEVC);预测并筛选了CTL、HTL和B细胞表位,评估其抗原性、免疫原性、MHC结合亲和力和人群覆盖率 (A4);将筛选的表位通过EAAAK、AAY、GPGPG和KK连接子连接,并与β-防御素佐剂融合 (A5);对构建体进行理化特性表征、结构建模、分子对接、分子动力学模拟、免疫模拟、密码子优化及体外克隆 (A6) 的评估。
analysis_zh.contribution: 体外计算结果表明,MEVC 具有良好的预测免疫原性、结构稳定性、广泛的人群覆盖率和表达潜力,支持将其作为针对 汉坦病毒 感染的预防性策略进行实验验证 (A14, A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要和补充信息;实验验证、体内免疫原性及安全性数据未报告 (A16)。

papers.title: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations
papers.abstract: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository.
