papers.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted Records The extraction sheets are not edited after extraction. Corrections are listed in tables in the repository, each with its source in the paper: 3,243 corrections to individual values, 331 deleted rows and 316 re-extracted rows. The pipeline downloads the sheets and applies the corrections to the downloaded copy. It stops if a value in a sheet no longer matches the value a correction expects, so a correction cannot silently overwrite a later change. 3.2.2 Metadata Consolidation Raw extractions are aggregated to consolidate citation metadata and establish unique identifiers for all studies, hosts, pathogens, and sequences. Because historical literature reports temporal data in highly variable formats (e.g., specific days, month-year, multi-year spans), a parsing function was developed to translate verbatim event dates into standardised start_date and end_date bounds, generating a consistent temporal_resolution flag for every record. 3.2.3 Taxonomic and Spatial Resolution Host taxonomy is resolved via the taxize package (Chamberlain et al. 2020), querying the GBIF API to append standardised hierarchies (Species through Class) and persistent taxonID keys (Chamberlain et al. 2026). Concurrently, geographical point data undergo validation against standard administrative boundaries. Coordinates are matched to their corresponding ISO-3166 country codes, and a spatial join against the Database of Global Administrative Areas (GADM, version 4.1) enriches each record with standardised sub- national administrative levels (adm1, adm2, adm3) relevant to the level of geographic resolution (Database of Global Administrative Areas 2022; Hijmans et al. 2024). Where a paper gave no coordinates, the named locality (a village, town or administrative unit) was located using Google Maps, Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap or the GEOnet Names Server, and coordinate_resolution_processed records the level of that locality. One study gives its sites only as GADM version 2.8 municipality identifiers (Wang et al. 2023); these records are placed at a point inside each municipality. 3.2.4 Trapping Effort To support downstream macro-ecological modelling, unstructured, free-text trapping descriptions are parsed to extract trap-night metrics, recorded in trap_nights_clean and described by trap_nights_status. Where source manuscripts reported data in tabular form listing multiple species and sampling sites, zero-detection records were extracted directly from blank or absent cells, preserving the structure of the original study design. Users should be aware that a zero-detection record in host_occurrences reflects a recorded absence within a specific sample, and should not be interpreted as ecological absence from the broader study area. 3.2.5 Pathogen and Genomic Enrichment Pathogen nomenclature undergoes parallel harmonisation against the NCBI Taxonomy database (Schoch et al. 2020). To bridge the gap between ecological sampling and molecular epidemiology, raw NCBI GenBank accession numbers extracted from the literature are passed back through the NCBI Entrez API (Sayers et al. 2024). This automated sequence enrichment downloads and parses the metadata for each accession. The host and pathogen names in each GenBank record are then compared with the names assigned in ArHa, and the differences are listed in the quality assurance report. Differences are not corrected automatically, because GenBank host metadata are often incomplete or give a synonym, an older name or a higher taxon (see Technical Validation). 3.2.6 Cross-study Duplicate Resolution Some field data were published in more than one paper and so entered ArHa more than once. After enrichment, the pipeline resolves these cases from a table of decisions in the processing scripts. Records are removed where a paper repeats data already extracted from another, merged where two papers report complementary results for the same animals, and linked as a duplicate group where the same animals are reported at different spatial or temporal breakdowns that cannot be reconciled (duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events). How the duplicates were found, and how many, is described below. 3.2.7 Quality Assurance and Schema Formatting Prior to final compilation, the pipeline generates a quality assurance report to evaluate database dimensions, coordinate validity, and taxonomic consistency. The final output is then structured into the four-tier relational schema. 3.3 Duplicate Publication of Field Data The same field data may be published more than once: a survey reported in several papers, a synthesis that consolidates earlier studies, or results reanalysed in a later paper. Where a paper does not say that its data have been published before, extraction can duplicate data. The same animals, sites and assay results then enter the database more than once, affecting subsequent counts, prevalences and ranges drawn from, in ways that cannot be seen in the data. To find such cases, each assay record was given a fingerprint of host species, pathogen, number positive, number tested and country, and pairs of studies that shared these fingerprints with overlapping sampling dates were flagged; study totals were compared in the same way. Each flagged pair was checked against both papers. Of the 44 pairs checked, 19 shared counts by chance. The rest were resolved by pre-defined rules: keep the most complete source data; where two papers report the same animals at breakdowns that cannot be merged, keep both and link them; and do not treat a review, or a second copy of the same paper, as a source. In all, 15 studies were removed entirely. Of these, 5 were one paper entered under two citation records. A further 124 host records were removed where two papers overlapped in part, and 43 host records were merged where two papers reported different assays on the same animals. Studies reporting the same animals in formats that cannot be merged are retained and linked through duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events: 6 studies in 3 groups (see Usage Notes). Each action is listed in the processing scripts and summarised in duplicate_resolution.csv. 3.4 The ArHa Database Explorer To visualise the relational data architecture and improve accessibility for the wider ecological and public health communities, the database is accompanied by the ArHa Database Explorer (https://diddrog11.shinyapps.io/arenavirus_hantavirus_app/). Built using R and Shiny (Chang et al. 2025), with a DuckDB backend (Mühleisen and Raasveldt 2025) for relational querying and Leaflet/plotly for interactive spatial and statistical visualisation (Cheng et al. 2024; Sievert 2020). Users can spatially visualise genomic sampling via the Leaflet integration, cross-filter by diagnostic modality or host taxonomy, and export subsets of the data for local modelling. 3.5 Data Records The ArHa database is released under a dual-format strategy to maximise utility and interoperability. This release holds 710 studies with sampling in 103 countries at 4,910 distinct localities (Figure 1). Sampling began between 1964 and 2021 (Figure 2). Figure 1: Sampling localities in ArHa, coloured by the resolution of the reported location. Each point is a distinct coordinate; a coordinate used at more than one resolution is shown at its most precise. The numbers in the legend are localities. Figure 2: Contents of ArHa. (a) Studies by the year in which sampling began, for the 689 of 710 studies that report a sampling date. (b) Host records by order. (c) Assay records for Arenaviridae and Hantaviridae by assay type; “Other or not reported” includes virus culture, sequencing, Western blot and pooled serology or PCR. 106 assay records for other or unrecorded virus families are not shown. Host occurrence records tend not to be individual animals. Each record gives the number of animals of one taxon recorded in one sampling session at one locality, and 14,333 records (26.3%) record that a taxon was not caught (individualCount = 0). Records are also unevenly spread across studies: the three studies with the most records, two long- term population studies and one survey of many localities, hold 52% of host_occurrences (Mariën et al. 2020; Cuypers et al. 2023; Guzzetta et al. 2017). Cuypers et al. (2023), for example, sampled 187 localities in Tanzania and reported results for 54 small mammal taxa at each, contributing 10,120 records (18.6% of host_occurrences) from 1,224 animals. Most of these records document that a taxon was not caught at a locality rather than a capture. Analyses that treat records as equivalent units, without reference to individualCount, will therefore over-weight studies of this kind relative to those that report only captures. 3.5.1 Schema Definition A primary vulnerability when archiving complex ecological sampling in flat-file formats is data expansion: forcing many-to-many relationships (e.g., multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host) into a single two-dimensional table can result in substantial record duplication. To mitigate this and ensure data integrity, the ArHa dataset is engineered as a four-tier relational database, summarised in Table 1 and Figure 3. Figure 3: The four relational tables of ArHa, their roles in the Darwin Core Archive, their keys and the number of records. Arrows run from the referenced table to the table that holds the key. Assay records link to a sampling event and, where the paper allows, to a host record; sequence records link to either a host or an assay record. Table 1: Summary of the four ArHa relational tables. full_text_sections.full_text: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations David Simons1, Ricardo Rivero2, Grant Rickard2, Ana Martinez-Checa3, Harry Gordon4, Gregory C. Milne3, David W. Redding3, Stephanie N. Seifert2 1 Department of Anthropology, Pennsylvania State University, State College, Pennsylvania, USA 2 Paul G. Allen School of Global Health, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA 3 Science Department, Natural History Museum, London, UK 4 School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich, UK Corresponding Authors: David Simons (dzs6259@psu.edu) and Stephanie N. Seifert (stephanie.seifert@wsu.edu) 1. Abstract Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted R…

papers.title: Rational Design of Candidate Hantavirus Gc Fusion Inhibitors Through Structure-Activity Relationship Analysis
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. Residues 308-320 undergo a non-uniform transition: the segments 308-311 and 318-320 preserved their internal geometry (span changes +0.4 Å and + 0.7 Å) while the central segment contracted sharply (313-317: 11.9 -> 6.1 Å). The selected pocket, bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 therefore spans a rigid anchoring region and an adjacent deformation zone. A library of approximately three million compounds was reduced to 1,041 docking-ready ligands and docked against prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity -5.35 kcal/mol). Two parent scaffolds (compounds 512 and 74) were carried into 38 analogues (SAR-v1-v20; MR-v1-v18) across a four node decomposition of the pocket. Each was redocked 10 times and assessed by DBSCAN pose clustering, a Gaussian residue contact fingerprint, an ensemble pose-drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after a short time scale relaxation (2 failed to parameterize). No significant pairwise correlations were detected among the three ranking criteria (residue-contact score versus MM/GBSA, Spearman ρ = 0.09, p = 0.59), so none was treated as decisive. SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. Residues 308-320 undergo a non-uniform transition: the segments 308-311 and 318-320 preserved their internal geometry (span changes +0.4 Å and + 0.7 Å) while the central segment contracted sharply (313-317: 11.9 -> 6.1 Å). The selected pocket, bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 therefore spans a rigid anchoring region and an adjacent deformation zone. A library of approximately three million compounds was reduced to 1,041 docking-ready ligands and docked against prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity -5.35 kcal/mol). Two parent scaffolds (compounds 512 and 74) were carried into 38 analogues (SAR-v1-v20; MR-v1-v18) across a four node decomposition of the pocket. Each was redocked 10 times and assessed by DBSCAN pose clustering, a Gaussian residue contact fingerprint, an ensemble pose-drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after a short time scale relaxation (2 failed to parameterize). No significant pairwise correlations were detected among the three ranking criteria (residue-contact score versus MM/GBSA, Spearman ρ = 0.09, p = 0.59), so none was treated as decisive. SAR-v17 ranked first of 38 by weighted residue-contact score, ninth of 36 by MM/GBSA (-11.08 kcal/mol) and fifteenth of 38 by ensemble drift (0.094 Å), all ten poses fell within a single DBSCAN cluster. It was the analouge with the best mean rank among the SAR and MR series. SAR-v20 was retained as a comparator because it only differed in structure to SAR-v17 by a single atom. All findings are predictions; no binding, fusion-inhibition or antiviral assay has been performed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe disease and lack targeted antivirals. Methods: A prefusion Gc pocket was defined by structural comparison, a ~3 million‑compound library was filtered to 1,041 ligands and docked, and two scaffolds were expanded to 38 analogues evaluated by clustering, residue‑contact scoring, drift index, and MM/GBSA. Results: The library showed a mean predicted affinity of –5.35 kcal/mol; SAR‑v17 ranked highest by residue‑contact score and performed well in MM/GBSA (–11.08 kcal/mol) and drift metrics. Contribution: The work provides computational Gc fusion‑inhibitor candidates and a SAR pipeline for future testing. Limitations: No experimental binding or antiviral assays were conducted and only an abstract is available.

papers.title: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness.

INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. Despite growing research on hantavirus epidemiology, reservoir ecology, occupational exposure, and diagnostic techniques, important gaps remain in the integration of clinical laboratory preparedness and biosafety within hantavirus response systems [12]. Current international guidance emphasizes that laboratory confirmation requires appropriate serological or molecular testing, while potentially infectious specimens must be handled, packaged, transported, and processed under risk-appropriate containment conditions [1]. However, preparedness also depends on trained personnel, quality-management systems, validated procedures, referral networks, and sufficient resources. A recent Asia-Pacific assessment involving substantial participation from Philippine laboratories identified staff-training and budget limitations among the major barriers to strengthening laboratory quality and competence, indicating broader system-level constraints that may also affect preparedness for uncommon emerging pathogens [19]. These limitations are particularly relevant to hantavirus preparedness in the Philippines. In June 2026, the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine issued specific instructions for the collection, handling, packaging, transport, and referral of specimens from suspected hantavirus cases, emphasizing personnel safety, specimen integrity, coordination with designated reference laboratories, and compliance with biosafety and biosecurity standards [18]. Nevertheless, the existence of national referral guidance does not necessarily indicate that hantavirus testing and biosafety procedures are routinely implemented across hospital and clinical laboratories. Thus, limited evidence regarding decentralized diagnostic capacity, laboratory personnel competency, quality assurance, containment practices, and functional referral pathways represents an important knowledge gap. Systematically evaluating these areas is necessary to determine how effectively Philippine laboratories could recognize suspected hantavirus infections and safely manage and refer to associated clinical specimens, while drawing lessons from laboratory systems in other countries. . Therefore, this systematic review aims to evaluate diagnostic preparedness and biosafety measures for hantavirus infections in clinical laboratories, with particular consideration of their applicability to the Philippines. Specifically, it seeks to identify and compare diagnostic methods used for hantavirus detection; assess laboratory preparedness, testing capacity, quality assurance, and specimen-referral systems; evaluate biosafety measures for specimen collection, processing, transport, storage, and disposal; compare practices across countries and resource settings; identify major diagnostic and biosafety gaps; and determine evidence-based strategies that may strengthen hantavirus laboratory preparedness in the Philippines and comparable resource-limited settings. METHODOLOGY 2.1Study Design and Reporting Framework This study employed a systematic review design to identify, evaluate, and synthesize available evidence on hantavirus infection, with particular attention to epidemiology, human exposure, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, biosafety, and implications for public health and laboratory preparedness in the Philippines. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [20]. A structured approach was applied to literature identification, screening and eligibility assessment, data extraction, methodological appraisal, and evidence synthesis. The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [39] under registration number CRD420261485094. Given the heterogeneity of the included evidence in terms of study design, geographical setting, study populations, diagnostic approaches, exposure measures, and reported outcomes, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, findings were synthesized using a narrative and thematic approach, allowing evidence to be organized and interpreted across the major domains addressed by the review. 2.2 Literature Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies relevant to hantavirus infection and its epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, ecological, and public health dimensions. The principal electronic databases searched were PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Supplementary searches were undertaken through manual screening of reference lists and relevant institutional and research repositories. Grey literature and technical documents from recognized public health organizations and national agencies were also considered when they contributed directly to the objectives of the review. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and included terms related to Hantavirus, Orthohantavirus, human–rodent interaction, zoonotic transmission, occupational exposure, seroprevalence, reservoir surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, and public health. An example of the search strategy was: (Hantavirus or Orthohantavirus) and (occupational exposure or human–rodent interface or zoonotic transmission) and (seroprevalence or reservoir surveillance or public health) Search terms were modified where necessary to accommodate the indexing systems and search functions of individual databases. 2.3 Eligibility Criteria Studies were considered eligible when they provided evidence relevant to hantavirus infection or transmission, including human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical disease, laboratory diagnosis, occupational or environmental risk, rodent reservoirs, ecological or molecular surveillance, outbreaks, biosafety, or public health implications. Eligible evidence included observational studies such as cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies, as well as outbreak investigations, seroepidemiological studies, ecological and molecular surveillance studies, and other relevant primary investigations. Selected authoritative technical and public health documents were considered when they provided information directly relevant to laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, biosafety, or preparedness. Studies were excluded when they were unrelated to the objectives of the review, provided insufficient information for meaningful interpretation, represented duplicate publications, consisted primarily of opinion or editorial material, or could not provide adequate information for eligibility assessment. The initial search identified 304 records. Duplicate records were removed before screening, after which titles and abstracts were evaluated against the predetermined eligibility criteria. Potentially relevant publications were subsequently assessed through full-text review. Studies that did not satisfy the eligibility criteria at the full-text stage were excluded, with the principal reasons for exclusion documented. Following completion of the screening and eligibility assessment, 18 studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for the final systematic review. The study-selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram showing the progression of records through identification, duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, exclusion, and final inclusion. 2.5 Data Extraction Relevant information was systematically extracted from each included study using a structured data-extraction approach. Extracted variables included, where applicable, the author and year of publication, country or geographical setting, study design, study population or sample, sample size, hantavirus species or strain, diagnostic or laboratory method, exposure or reservoir characteristics, principal findings, and implications for clinical practice, laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, or public health. Particular attention was given to findings relevant to human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, rodent reservoirs, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental risks, and biosafety or laboratory preparedness. The appraisal focused on the clarity of the study objectives, appropriateness of study design and participant or specimen selection, adequacy of sample size and methodology, reliability of diagnostic or laboratory procedures, completeness of outcome reporting, and potential sources of selection, measurement, and reporting bias. full_text_sections.full_text: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review Journal Name: Annals of Medical and Health Research: An International Journal DOI: https://doi.org/10.51470/ARMHR.2026.5.1.104 Keywords: Hantavirus, laboratory preparedness, biosafety, molecular diagnosis, serological diagnosis, One Health, surveillance, Philippines Abstract Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness. INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. papers.title: SARS, H1N1, EBOLA, COVID-19, MPOX, H5N1 AND HANTAVIRUS: IS HUMANITY ENTERING A NEW ERA OF PANDEMIC? IS TÜRKİYE PREPARED FOR THE NEXT GLOBAL OUTBREAK?
papers.abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases pose persistent challenges to global health security. Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.

Sebla AK*1 1VM Medical Park Maltepe Hospital Patient Rights Unit, Istanbul, Türkiye * Corresponding author; sebla.ak@gmail.com Abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases pose persistent challenges to global health security. Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community- based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats. Keywords: One Health, Pandemic preparedness, Turkish healthcare system, Zoonotic diseases Received: June 11, 2026 Accepted: October 16, 2026 1. Introduction Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases continue to challenge global health security, demonstrating the need for sustained preparedness beyond individual epidemic events. Outbreaks of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), together with renewed concerns about avian influenza A(H5N1) and hantavirus infections, illustrate the diverse and evolving nature of infectious disease threats. The risk of future outbreaks is shaped by interconnected factors, including environmental change, biodiversity loss, urbanization, international travel, and increased interactions between humans, animals, and their shared environments. Consequently, pandemic preparedness requires more than adequate clinical capacity; it Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 271 also depends on effective surveillance, timely risk assessment, intersectoral coordination, and international cooperation. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed substantial differences in countries’ capacities to prevent, detect, and respond to public health emergencies, reinforcing the importance of strengthening preparedness at both national and global levels. The adoption of the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement in 2025 further underscored international efforts to improve pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response [1]. The emergence of zoonotic diseases is closely associated with ecological and environmental changes that alter interactions among humans, wildlife, and domestic animals. Evidence indicates that zoonotic host diversity can increase in human-dominated ecosystems, while climate change may alter opportunities for viral transmission between species [2], [3]. These findings reinforce the importance of understanding infectious disease emergence through an integrated perspective rather than considering human health in isolation. The One Health approach provides a framework for addressing the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health and has been increasingly emphasized in research on emerging infectious diseases and pandemic preparedness [4], [5]. Against this background, this study examines major infectious disease outbreaks with global public health implications, considers factors that may contribute to future pandemic risks, and assesses Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future outbreaks using a SWOT analysis framework. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Research Type This study employed a descriptive review design based on a structured literature search and document analysis. The review examined scientific publications and official institutional documents concerning major infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic risks, and pandemic preparedness, with particular emphasis on Türkiye’s healthcare system. The review was not designed as a systematic review; rather, it aimed to synthesize relevant documentary evidence and interpret the findings using a SWOT framework. The analysis focused on identifying reported healthcare capacities, structural challenges, opportunities for improvement, and potential threats to Türkiye’s preparedness for future global outbreaks. 2.2. Data Sources This study was based exclusively on secondary sources and did not involve primary data collection or direct interaction with human participants. The sources included scientific publications and official reports from the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), as well as other relevant institutional documents and peer-reviewed publications. 2.3. Literature Search Strategy and Eligibility Criteria The review included scientific publications and official institutional documents addressing major infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic risks, and pandemic preparedness, with particular emphasis on Türkiye’s healthcare system. Eligible sources were required to provide relevant information on disease emergence, outbreak management, surveillance, healthcare system capacity, or pandemic preparedness. Peer-reviewed articles, official reports, and relevant institutional documents were considered for inclusion. Duplicate records, sources with insufficient methodological information, and publications unrelated to the study objectives were excluded. The review focused on seven disease groups identified in the study title: SARS, influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, COVID-19, mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections. Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 272 2.4. Document Review Procedure Data were collected through the examination of scientific publications and official institutional documents. The reviewed sources were assessed for information concerning disease characteristics, outbreak management, surveillance systems, healthcare infrastructure, and national and international pandemic preparedness. Relevant information was recorded and organized according to its relevance to the study objectives and the SWOT framework. No primary data collection instrument was used because the study relied exclusively on secondary sources. 2.5. Literature Search and Selection Process The literature search covered publications from 2002 to 2026. Sources were identified through searches of publications and reports issued by the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, the YÖK National Thesis Center, TR Index (ULAKBİM), the TÜBİTAK ULAKBİM Medical Database, DergiPark, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Türk Medline, and Google Scholar. Search terms included “pandemic preparedness,” “zoonotic diseases,” “One Health,” “Turkish healthcare system,” “SARS,” “H1N1,” “Ebola,” “COVID-19,” “Mpox,” “H5N1,” and “Hantavirus.” These terms were used individually and in combination, where appropriate. Records were assessed for relevance to the study objectives, publication type, and contribution to the understanding of pandemic preparedness and zoonotic disease risks. Duplicate records, publications with insufficient methodological information, and sources unrelated to the research objectives were excluded. 2.6. Data Analysis The included documents were analyzed qualitatively using a descriptive approach. Relevant information concerning Türkiye’s preparedness for emerging infectious diseases and future pandemics was identified and organized according to the study objectives. The extracted information was classified into four SWOT categories: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Strengths and weaknesses represented reported internal capacities and challenges of the healthcare and preparedness systems, whereas opportunities and threats represented external developments and conditions that could influence preparedness. The resulting categories were interpreted in relation to the documentary evidence reviewed. This approach provided the analytical basis for the SWOT findings presented in the Results section. 3. Results 3.1. SWOT Analysis for Türkiye 3.1.1 Strengths • Strengthened public health infrastructure and outbreak management experience following COVID-19 • Advanced laboratory capacity and widespread molecular diagnostic methods • Digital surveillance and infectious disease monitoring systems operated by the Ministry of Health • Experience gained in filiation and contact tracing practices • Extensive hospital network and high intensive care capacity • Increasing academic interest in the One Health approach • Improved emergency management capacity after COVID-19 • Strengthened vaccine and pharmaceutical logistics infrastructure Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 273 3.1.2 Weaknesses • Insufficient zoonotic disease surveillance systems • Deficiencies in rodent population control • Limited public awareness regarding zoonotic infections • Biosafety challenges in rural areas • Limited implementation of the One Health approach • Healthcare workforce shortages and burnout risks • Inadequate virus-specific national preparedness and emergency response plans 3.1.3 Opportunities • Increased healthcare investments after COVID-19 • Expanding collaborations with WHO and international organizations • Development of artificial intelligence–supported epidemiological surveillance systems • Increasing cooperation between universities and the Ministry of Health • Potential for developing digital early warning systems • Advancements in domestic vaccine and biotechnology production capacity • Integration potential of the One Health approach into national health policies • Increasing academic research on zoonotic diseases • Expansion of community-based public health education programs • Opportunities for integration among veterinary medicine, environmental health, and human health sectors 3.1.4 Threats • Increasing rodent populations associated with climate change • Emergence of new zoonotic diseases • Increased transmission risks associated with global travel and trade • Environmental hygiene problems in rural areas • Increased rodent exposure risks in agricultural settings • Delayed diagnosis and intervention in rare infectious diseases • Potential burden of global outbreaks on the healthcare system • Biological risks associated with international food trade and logistics • Misinformation and infodemic-related risks 4. Historical Development of Pandemic and Increasing Global Risk 4.1. SARS (2002-2003) Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) emerged in southern China in 2002 and spread internationally, demonstrating how rapidly an emerging infectious disease can cross national borders through international travel. The outbreak highlighted the importance of early case detection, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, and coordinated international surveillance. The outbreak was brought under control in 2003 following coordinated international surveillance and public health interventions, highlighting the importance of early detection, case identification, and infection control in containing emerging infectious diseases [6]. 4.2. Influenza A/H1N1 (Swine Flu) Pandemic (2009) Influenza A/H1N1 was a global influenza pandemic that emerged in 2009. Commonly referred to as “swine flu” because it was initially identified in pigs, the disease rapidly evolved into a global Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 274 pandemic due to its high transmissibility, despite having a lower mortality rate compared with SARS. Particularly high infection rates among young adults attracted considerable attention. Following the H1N1 pandemic, many countries updated their pandemic preparedness plans, strengthened influenza surveillance systems, and increased vaccine production capacity [7]. Today, H1N1 remains among the circulating seasonal influenza strains and continues to be monitored as an important global public health concern. WHO officially declared the H1N1 outbreak a pandemic in 2009 [7]. 4.3. Ebola Virus Disease Ebola virus disease is considered one of the deadliest viral hemorrhagic fevers of the modern era due to its high mortality rate and devastating impact on healthcare systems. The 2014–2016 West African outbreak caused not only severe health consequences but also major economic and social destruction. During the outbreak, infection among healthcare workers highlighted the critical importance of infection prevention and control measures [8]. Ebola outbreaks contributed significantly to strengthening the concept of global health security by promoting the development of early diagnosis systems, contact tracing, isolation practices, field epidemiology, and international coordination mechanisms. Although the development of effective vaccines represents substantial progress, Ebola remains a closely monitored infectious disease due to persistent zoonotic transmission risks and fragile healthcare infrastructures in parts of Africa [8]. 4.4. Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) Pandemic COVID-19 became the largest global health crisis of the modern era. The collapse of healthcare systems, shortages in intensive care capacity, disruptions in global supply chains, and vaccine inequities deepened the global consequences of the pandemic. COVID-19 demonstrated that healthcare systems should not be evaluated solely on the basis of hospital capacity. It also revealed the critical importance of data management, digital health technologies, early warning systems, and scientific coordination capacity [9]. 4.5. Mpox (Monkeypox) Mpox is a zoonotic viral infection that has become an important global health concern due to its increasing international spread in recent years. The 2022 global outbreak demonstrated that the disease was not limited to the African continent and could rapidly spread across regions through international travel and close-contact networks. During this period, contact tracing, isolation practices, and community-based awareness campaigns played critical roles in infection control [10]. The mpox outbreak also tested the preparedness of global healthcare systems against emerging infections in the post-COVID-19 era. Although the mortality rate of mpox is lower than that of Ebola or SARS, the disease remains a major public health concern because of its rapid transmission potential and burden on healthcare systems. In particular, insufficient surveillance systems and limited healthcare access in endemic African regions increase the risk of future outbreaks [10]. 4.6. Avian Influenza A/H5N1 (Bird Flu) The H5N1 influenza virus is among the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses and constitutes a major zoonotic threat with global transmission potential through bird populations. Although human infections are relatively rare, the virus causes major public health concerns because of its high mortality rate when transmission occurs. Migratory waterfowl, which serve as the primary reservoirs of the virus, play a critical role in intercontinental spread [11]. In recent years, the ability of H5N1 to infect certain mammalian species in addition to birds has been considered a serious warning regarding the virus’s adaptive capacity. This has raised concerns about the potential emergence of a new Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 275 influenza pandemic through mutations enabling human-to-human transmission. Consequently, WHO and other international health organizations continue to monitor H5N1 as a virus with high pandemic potential [11]. 4.7. Hantavirus Infection Hantaviruses are zoonotic viruses belonging to the Hantaviridae family. These viruses naturally circulate among rodents and are transmitted to humans through contact with infected rodent urine, feces, or saliva. Transmission generally occurs via aerosolized particles, particularly in rural areas and environments with dense rodent populations. analysis.summary_en: Background: The emergence and re‑emergence of infectious diseases such as SARS, H1N1, Ebola, COVID‑19, mpox, H5N1 and hantavirus continuously challenge global health security. Methods: A descriptive review was conducted using a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports, with findings organized through a SWOT framework. analysis_zh.results: 综述指出土耳其在医疗基础设施、重症监护能力、数字健康系统和COVID-19防控经验方面具有优势;挑战包括医务人员不足、动物源监测空白、公众卫生素养低、部门间协作薄弱以及依赖外部生物技术供应;气候变化、人员流动、迁徙和贸易被视为疾病出现的驱动因素;作者建议加强综合监测、One‐Health协同、国产疫苗/诊断产品生产以及社区教育。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究强调在土耳其对新发传染病威胁进行持续、多部门准备的重要性。

papers.title: Cuadro clínico y eventos inmunológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por variantes Sudamericanas de Hantavirus: revisión sistemática
papers.abstract: Objetivo. Analizar los mecanismos inmunopatológicos implicados en el desarrollo del HCPS y su correlación con la severidad de las manifestaciones clínicas de las variantes sudamericanas. Métodos. Se realizó una revisión sistemática de la literatura científica sobre la inmunopatogenia de hantavirus sudamericanos bajo los lineamientos PRISMA 2020. Desarrollo. Las variantes de Hantavirus en Bolivia (ANDV, RIOMV y LNV) desencadenan el HCPS. El virus infecta el endotelio sin destruirlo directamente. La variante AND evade la respuesta innata acumulando alta carga viral, mientras RIOMV hiperestimula macrófagos y perfil Th1/Th17. Esto desregula la permeabilidad capilar, causando edema pulmonar no cardiogénico y shock cardiogénico. Conclusiones. El síndrome es una enfermedad inmunomediada donde la severidad depende de la variante genética. El daño tisular no es lítico, sino el resultado de una respuesta inmune descontrolada y una tormenta de citocinas. Comprender esta inmunopatogenia es crucial para diseñar terapias dirigidas a regular la inflamación sistémica.
